## TL;DR

Completed a headless browser QA pass of Deployments, Dev, and Context using the auth-less server running from this isolated worktree. All visited pages rendered at 1280px and 375px with no horizontal overflow or observed browser errors. Exercised refresh and Context tab navigation, verified the deploy confirmation, and checked empty Dev and Docs states through browser-side API response interception. I did not confirm a real deployment push or start any configured dev command because those actions would have side effects. No reproducible UI bug was found, so there was no source change or regression test to add.

## Work and rationale

The assignment called for hands-on coverage of populated and empty states, controls, errors, and desktop/mobile widths. I read the task file and the UI conventions, confirmed this worktree was clean, built the UI, and started the prescribed `just serve-noauth 7272` server from the task worktree. I used only headless Playwright Chromium. This kept the evidence tied to the branch under review and honored the request not to open a visible browser or the user's Chrome.

On Deployments, the running project supplied genuine populated data: `prod` and `main` branches, service rows, branch distance, provider destinations, and environment binding messages. I used Refresh and observed the page return to its populated state. I opened the prod Deploy confirmation and inspected the copy: it named the remote push, affected services, current unpushed count, and commands. Since confirmation would cause a real push to a shared remote, I closed the dialog with Escape rather than executing it. I recorded the limitation plainly instead of describing an unperformed deployment as verified.

On Dev, the page showed five real configured targets, including server, build, and process types. Refresh worked and the Start actions were present. Those buttons launch project processes (some commands build or install applications), so I did not start one merely to mark a QA checklist complete. I intercepted the target-list API in the browser to provide an empty list and confirmed the page rendered its actionable setup guidance. The repository state was not changed to manufacture empty data.

On Context, I inspected the Docs tab with its selected `AGENTS.md`, then switched through Skills, Discover, History, and back to Docs. Skills and History showed data. Discover displayed “Loading Skills.sh…” at the time of observation, but there was no console error, uncaught exception, failed request, or proof that loading remained stuck, so I treated this as an observation instead of a defect. I injected an empty docs response in the browser and verified that “No docs found” and the selection prompt rendered at mobile width.

I checked document width against the viewport on each route at 1280px and 375px. Both widths matched, including for the empty Dev and Docs states. Browser listeners collected console errors, page errors, and failed requests across the passes; none were observed. Results and boundaries are in `docs/qa/2026-11-deployments-dev-context.md`.

## Approaches tried

I first attempted a generic `<main>` selector to read the page body for the empty-state probe. This app's layout does not expose that element, so Playwright waited until its timeout. I corrected the probe to use the actual `.main` app container and reran the states successfully. This was a QA-script selector mistake, not an application failure.

The server's real project data provided the populated scenarios. For empty Dev and Docs states, browser-side route interception isolated the UI from server configuration changes. I considered deployment data as an empty scenario, but the live project is configured and changing its TOML would be outside the acceptance scope and prohibited. I therefore reported that limitation instead of claiming the empty Deployments state had been inspected.

## Challenges and blockers

Two controls have real consequences: Deploy pushes a branch to a shared remote, and Dev Start launches a local process. QA could safely inspect the confirmation and the available controls, but could not execute those actions without creating side effects. No human approval or credentials were needed to render the pages, and no defect blocked completion of the read-only checks.

The Discover catalog was still in its loading presentation during the short pass. Since the browser reported no failed request and this session did not establish a persistent stall, I did not change code or label it a bug. A follow-up that specifically validates remote catalog completion may be useful if the loading state is reported elsewhere.

## Key learnings

The task worktree can run the repository's auth-less preview server independently, and its configured data makes the populated deployment and dev views representative. Browser-side response interception is a useful way to verify empty-state copy without mutating project configuration. For action controls with external consequences, the confirmation dialog itself is meaningful QA evidence, while clicking through the final confirmation would not be appropriate without explicit authorization. The app's page shell is `.main`, so future headless probes should target that rather than assume a semantic `<main>` element.
